transcript: Edward is not only the first play that I've seen this year, shockingly, but it's also my favourite play that I've seen in a while. Edward is a new play written and performed by Ed Schmidt, who brings to each show 27 objects owned by a man named Edward. And through these objects we get to learn little. bits and pieces of Edward's story. The audience gets to dictate the order of things by picking each object. And so we don't get a chronological portrayal of Edward. We get glimpses into Edward, little tiny anecdotes of who this man was. And from those anecdotes we get to paint together a complete picture, or as complete as we, the audience, get to paint, of a man that we've never met. Not only is Ed Schmidt an absolutely incredible storyteller, the way that he brings you in with each of these objects and each of these stories that he has to tell is incredible, but each of these stories is so uniquely written that you never know how much information you're going to get from each object. One object may give you what almost feels like a. A page in a planner, and one you get an in depth story into a piece of his life. And so much of this play reminded me of how we find out about people that we know, people that we meet in real life. You don't get to know all of them at once. You get To know them in anecdotes that they choose to tell you. And this is very much like that, except it's of a man who will never get to meet, and whose stories are now finite. Not only that, but Edward is a site specific play, and so it was originally performed in apartments. Now it's being performed at bookstores. And so I saw this at Powerhouse Arena in Brooklyn, and because of this location, it is incredibly intimate. You only had about 20 other audience members with you. Everybody got to pick at least one, sometimes even more objects. And so it almost feels like you're gathered at a party and hearing somebody tell a story of a friend. And there's something to be said about the intimacy of this play. And you could tell that the storytelling was really great, because powerhouse Arena is right next to an above ground subway, and so we would get it, a subway pass by pretty loudly every like 10 to 15 minutes. And yet I was always locked in to each of these stories. I honestly cannot recommend the show enough. Unfortunately, the entire run right now is sold out. However, occasionally they'll have a cancellation ticket pop up. You can put yourself on a wait list. And I definitely, highly recommend following Ed Schmidt and seeing if they do any more of these shows in the future. This already is not the first run. He previously performed this in apartments. And With how fast this sold out, I can't imagine that we won't get more dates in the future, so definitely keep an eye out on this one. Truly a gem of a piece of theatre. As far as tickets go, it's pretty affordable. Full price is $40, which for this intimate of a show and this high of a demand is unheard of. If you can go see it, I highly recommend.
